headline: Peconic settles into the mid-70s — porgies stacked at Shelter Island, weakfish riding the bunker into the coves
subhead: A cooling southerly knocked the edge off the heat and woke up the bottom bite exactly like the bay usually does this time of year.
body_markdown:
By the first week of August the Peconic has settled into its deep-summer rhythm, and if you've fished these waters as long as I have you can practically set your watch by it. Water temps are sitting in the mid-70s across the bay proper, warmer in the shallow coves off Noyack and Three Mile Harbor, a touch cooler out toward the Race where Gardiners Bay starts feeling the pull of Plum Gut current. That front that pushed through midweek brought a stiff southerly and roughed up the surface for a day, but behind it the water dropped a degree or two — and just like I figured it would, that knocked the porgies and fluke into gear again. We flagged that exact pattern a few days back, and it played out almost to the letter: the Peconic takes a southerly a lot better than the ocean beaches do, and the bay bounced right back with a stronger daytime bite than we'd had the week before.

Shelter Island is doing what Shelter Island does in August — porgies thick around the reef structure off Cornelius Point, the rips under the Route 114 bridge, and the drop-offs outside Coecles Harbor. Anchor up in 15 to 25 feet, get a chum pot of ground clam or mussel going, and fish small hooks with squid strips or sandworm on a high-low rig. These porgy have been running a good average size this month, plenty in the 12 to 14 inch class with a few chunkier fish mixed in on the slower tides. Best window is the last two hours of the incoming into the top of high — the current slows enough that the chum holds together and the fish stack up instead of scattering.

Fluke are exactly where they should be for this point in the season — off the shallow flats and into the channels where the bottom stays workable. The North Race, the edge of the Jessup's Neck channel, and the deeper cuts around Robins Island have all been giving up keeper fish on the drift. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, worked slow along bottom in 20 to 30 feet, are getting it done, and a few boats have done well tipping bucktails with a strip of squid for extra scent when the current's light. Outgoing tide has been the better call — it pulls bait out of the shallows and concentrates the fluke along the channel edges where they're waiting.

Weakfish are the story worth watching right now. We said back at the start of the month that they'd track the peanut bunker into the bays through August, and that's precisely what's happening — schools of peanuts are pushing into Noyack Bay and the mouth of Sag Harbor Cove, and the weakfish are right behind them, holding in the deeper holes, 15 to 20 feet, working the tide changes morning and evening. Small bucktails or bunker-imitation soft plastics, fished slow near bottom, have been picking off fish in the 3 to 5 pound range. They're not schooled up thick everywhere, so it pays to move around and find where the peanuts are balled — the birds working the surface will usually tell you before your fishfinder does.

Bluefish are riding that same bunker distribution, and the cocktail blues have started showing in the back bays right on schedule — Three Mile Harbor and the creeks off Northwest have both had pods of snapper-to-cocktail blues chopping at peanut bunker on the surface in the early morning. Light tackle, small metals or a Gulp shad on a jighead, and you can have steady action for an hour before the sun gets too high and they slide off.

Striped bass have gone the way stripers always go once the bay settles into the mid-70s — they've pulled off the flats and into deeper, cooler structure, and the best action now is a nighttime game. Channel edges around Orient Point and the deeper holes toward Plum Gut are holding fish that are feeding hard after dark on bunker chunks and eels fished on the bottom. Daytime, your best shot is right around the tide change when moving water pulls bait past the deeper rips — I've had better luck working the last hour of the ebb into the turn than blind-casting the flats at noon.

Looking ahead, if this stable, southerly-leaning pattern holds, I'd expect the porgy and fluke bite to stay solid through the coming week, with the weakfish continuing to build as more peanut bunker pushes into the coves. Keep an eye on Gardiners Bay and the water off Orient as we move deeper into August — the current through Plum Gut is starting to carry more bait, and that's usually the first sign the fall transition is loading up, even if it's still weeks away. For now, work the tides, keep your baits small and natural, and don't sleep on that early-morning window before the sun climbs — that's where the bay's showing its best cards right now.
